title: Angels We Have Heard on High
description: The French carol "Les anges dans nos campagnes" in its English words, for 2 to 4 singers: three verses, each ending in the long rolling "Gloria in excelsis Deo". The tune and words as Charles L. Hutchins printed them in Carols Old and Carols New (1916); the alto, tenor and bass are our own, on the harmony of his page.

credits.words: English words attributed to James Chadwick (by 1862), from the French carol "Les anges dans nos campagnes"

licence.words: public domain: James Chadwick died 1882; the earliest known printings of these English words are in London, 1862 (The Crown of Jesus) and 1864 (The Crown of Jesus Music)
licence.tune: public domain: a traditional French carol tune; its earliest known printing is in Paris in 1842 (Choix de cantiques sur des airs nouveaux), and with these English words in London in 1864 (The Crown of Jesus Music)
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella: our own alto, tenor and bass under the tune as Hutchins printed it, checked against the chords of his page's four-part setting, which is unsigned and so was not copied; the chords are his or near relatives (a D for his suspended chord on "heard", a held G, A minor and D7 over A under the Gloria's falling notes), chosen so the alto keeps the third for 2 and 3 singers and each line moves by step; every voice sings "Glo-" through the Gloria, the lower parts one held note a chord (Hutchins marks the Gloria "Unison ad lib."); the alto crosses a third above the tune's low D on "ri-a"; breaths written in for beginners; the tenor climbs G3, B3, E4, D4 into each Gloria (beats 32 to 40), so it never moves in octaves with the tune; accepted exceptions: every part holds "Glo-" through the long Gloria run on one note a chord, as Hutchins marks it "Unison ad lib."; the alto's octave B3 to B4 into each Gloria (beats 30 to 32), the same note after a rest, keeping the third at both ends; and the alto on the D7's seventh, C, falling to B, where the duet and trio lack the third on quaver passing chords and at each "De-o" cadence (the tenor has it at 4)
licence.source: Charles L. Hutchins, ed., Carols Old and Carols New, for Use at Christmas and Other Seasons of the Christian Year (Boston: The Parish Choir, 1916), Carol 181, "Angels we have heard" (Christmas), "Old French Carol", p. 157, in four parts in F, 4/4, written here a tone higher in G; verses 1 to 3 of the four as printed (verse 1 under the music, 2 and 3 below it), the refrain once a verse as printed; Princeton Theological Seminary Library copy, archive.org/details/carolsoldcarolsn00huth (leaf n182). The earliest known printing of the same plates is Hutchins's weekly The Parish Choir, No. 543 (Boston, 11 November 1891), copyright 1891 by C. L. Hutchins. The tune's pitches and rhythm are Hutchins's except that each two-bar line's closing minim is sung as a crotchet and a breath (as is "a" before "in excelsis"), and the last "o" of verse 3 is held four beats, not six, so the song ends on its bar line. Checked against The Catholic Church Hymnal with Music (New York, 1905), No. 10, "Gloria in excelsis Deo", Old French Melody, p. 11 (hymnary.org, CCH1905 page 36), which prints the same tune with a closely similar unsigned four-part harmony.
